claims.claim:
“I don’t say this disparagingly — how could I? This movie went on to make millions of dollars. But I look at a movie like ‘F1’ and I’m like, ‘F1’ was made by AI. Wasn’t it? I mean, the structure was exactly the structure that you would learn in school. The actors say the lines exactly the way it would be written if a computer was writing exactly what would be the right thing for that time. And they were able to dominate the technology to make something big and beautiful and potentially where a lot of the information comes from other places.”

F1 was well-executed, zero-perplexity, hallucination-filled not-technically-AI slop. Brad Pitt does the Brad Pitt thing and oozes cool. The people liked it.

I say ‘not technically AI’ because it was made by an intelligence that was rather artificial in its own way, except it was instantiated inside humans.

I did not like F1, because it fell under my Obvious Slop waterline and the theoretical sport it was portraying, that is very different from F1, was neither coherent nor safe. Jodie Foster is correct, as is the parallel to AI.

A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer

There was a huge cheating scandal at Brown, where 50 students were caught cheating on the economic math final. Does Professor Serrano know where he went wrong?

Manuel G. Pascual: This year, the economist decided that both the midterm and the final exams for his course would be of the take-home, closed-book type (there is a certain tradition of this at Ivy League schools). “It’s a very nice kind of exam, because as you’re giving students practically unlimited time to complete it, it lets you make it harder than normal, to see how far they can go.”

… But it also hurts him that the one time in 34 years that he decided to offer a take-home exam, for highly justified reasons, the response was wide-scale fraud.

Oh. Yeah, sorry, you can’t do that anymore.

claims.claim:
Giving people tools with which to learn often doesn’t cause learning. Another classic example is ‘put a lot of MIT classes online for free.’ MIT did this, no one noticed, those who noticed did not use the classes to learn.

Ryan Brewer: It’s shocking to me that LLMs didn’t create an educational renaissance. Shouldn’t I be able to learn a language in a month? What did we get wrong?

Yishan: Because it’s not about what the teacher can do, it’s what the student can do.

Learning is energetically expensive and the brain doesn’t want to do it. All educational systems are methods to motivate, trick, or force brains into learning.

(You can make AI systems to do this, but it’s still a couple steps away from just “AI is good at explaining things”)

+ work is a fixed amount

claims.claim:
The true versions of the claims:

Work expands to fill the time allotted, with decreasing marginal returns.

Machines doing too many of the tasks means loss of the particular job in question.

Controlling for quality of the thing, cheaper things get used more, and total amount paid can go up or go down.

Labor is paid well if and only if it is the scarce resource, which it may not be.

Abundant intelligence increasingly removes human cognitive work, and can potentially lead to machines that increasingly remove human physical work.

Renting generic intelligence may or may not be part of a winning strategy, but paying to develop specialized intelligence likely gets you bitter lesson pilled.

I did not like F1, because it fell under my Obvious Slop waterline and the theoretical sport it was portraying, that is very different from F1, was neither coherent nor safe. Jodie Foster is correct, as is the parallel to AI.
passages.why: F1 as AI-like slop

passages.text:
One possibility is this leads to bifurcation.

If you are making a generic low-perplexity movie or other piece of media, you can let the AI cook, and you will get your delicious pile of slop.

If you are making a high-perplexity movie or other piece of media, that works with its restrictions and says and does actual things, then you will use AI at most with caution, and part of the experience will be knowing it is not AI.
passages.why: Predicted split in AI media

Which way, modern man?

claims.claim:
Giving people tools with which to learn often doesn’t cause learning. Another classic example is ‘put a lot of MIT classes online for free.’ MIT did this, no one noticed, those who noticed did not use the classes to learn.

Ryan Brewer: It’s shocking to me that LLMs didn’t create an educational renaissance. Shouldn’t I be able to learn a language in a month? What did we get wrong?

Yishan: Because it’s not about what the teacher can do, it’s what the student can do.

Learning is energetically expensive and the brain doesn’t want to do it. All educational systems are methods to motivate, trick, or force brains into learning.

(You can make AI systems to do this, but it’s still a couple steps away from just “AI is good at explaining things”)

Ryan Brewer: I’m looking at my little sister’s high school class now, and i guess it just seems like all motivation to learn anything has gone completely out the window. Those who are genuinely curious people will 10-100x their ability to learn. The opposite however is also true, the bottom 95% of learners will use Chat to skip work completely. Just sad to see a tool like this be used to escape critical thought by all parties involved. Curious how we fix this

claims.claim:
Pizza: The internet gave every single person on Earth access to all of MIT’s lectures for free and I think most of us would agree that it hasn’t made us that much smarter. I don’t think the main problems and solutions here are technological.

All of YouTube, by contrast, did often make people either smarter or dumber, depending on how they used it, because it was far easier to use. MIT’s classes had too many trivial inconveniences and also tend to be actually quite hard.

If you want to learn a language in a month and are willing to put in the time and effort, you can probably do that right now, using a mixture of existing technology and LLMs. No one does it because no one both has that kind of time and wants to do that level of work.

claims.claim:
They Took Our Jobs

In response to the AI slop nonsense article from Chamath, Bryan Johnson tries to say the thing in actual human words.

Bryan Johnson: He's arguing that these knee jerk intuitions are wrong:

+ work is a fixed amount
+ machines doing tasks means lost jobs
+ cheaper things get used less
+ labor is the scarce resource
+ abundant intelligence removes human work
+ renting generic intelligence builds an edge

Elon Musk: AI+Robots will be able to do everything, resulting in universal high income. Work will be optional.

claims.claim:
The true versions of the claims:

Work expands to fill the time allotted, with decreasing marginal returns.

Machines doing too many of the tasks means loss of the particular job in question.

Controlling for quality of the thing, cheaper things get used more, and total amount paid can go up or go down.

Labor is paid well if and only if it is the scarce resource, which it may not be.

Abundant intelligence increasingly removes human cognitive work, and can potentially lead to machines that increasingly remove human physical work.

Renting generic intelligence may or may not be part of a winning strategy, but paying to develop specialized intelligence likely gets you bitter lesson pilled.

I would focus on ‘labor is the scarce resource.’

claims.claim:
Is AI already net killing jobs?

The lived experience and anecdotes say yes, at least at entry level. The economics types keep trying to quote statistics to try and say no.

Ara Kharazian: We can finally say AI isn't killing jobs.

A new paper from me, @tryramp , and @RevelioLabs uses firm-level spend and workforce data across 21K U.S. businesses to measure AI's impact on jobs.

Firms that adopt AI heavily grow headcount 10% over two years following adoption. Low adopters see no statistically significant change.

“I don’t say this disparagingly — how could I? This movie went on to make millions of dollars. But I look at a movie like ‘F1’ and I’m like, ‘F1’ was made by AI. Wasn’t it? I mean, the structure was exactly the structure that you would learn in school. The actors say the lines exactly the way it would be written if a computer was writing exactly what would be the right thing for that time. And they were able to dominate the technology to make something big and beautiful and potentially where a lot of the information comes from other places.”

F1 was well-executed, zero-perplexity, hallucination-filled not-technically-AI slop. Brad Pitt does the Brad Pitt thing and oozes cool. The people liked it.

I say ‘not technically AI’ because it was made by an intelligence that was rather artificial in its own way, except it was instantiated inside humans.

I did not like F1, because it fell under my Obvious Slop waterline and the theoretical sport it was portraying, that is very different from F1, was neither coherent nor safe. Jodie Foster is correct, as is the parallel to AI.
passages.why: F1 as AI-like slop

passages.text:
One possibility is this leads to bifurcation.

If you are making a generic low-perplexity movie or other piece of media, you can let the AI cook, and you will get your delicious pile of slop.

If you are making a high-perplexity movie or other piece of media, that works with its restrictions and says and does actual things, then you will use AI at most with caution, and part of the experience will be knowing it is not AI.
passages.why: Predicted media bifurcation

Right now, labor is a scarce resource. At a survivable wage, demand exceeds supply, even for many forms of relatively unskilled labor. Thus, the market wage is historically high, and there are many jobs.

What would happen if labor were no longer a scarce resource? Demand low, supply high. Market price goes down. Wages fall. Employment drops. Perhaps a lot. Duh.

claims.claim:
My central thesis on AI and education is:

LLMs are the best tool ever invented with which to learn things.

LLMs are also the best tool ever invented with which to not learn things.

Which way, modern man?

Giving people tools with which to learn often doesn’t cause learning. Another classic example is ‘put a lot of MIT classes online for free.’ MIT did this, no one noticed, those who noticed did not use the classes to learn.

Ryan Brewer: It’s shocking to me that LLMs didn’t create an educational renaissance. Shouldn’t I be able to learn a language in a month? What did we get wrong?

Yishan: Because it’s not about what the teacher can do, it’s what the student can do.

Learning is energetically expensive and the brain doesn’t want to do it. All educational systems are methods to motivate, trick, or force brains into learning.

(You can make AI systems to do this, but it’s still a couple steps away from just “AI is good at explaining things”)

Ryan Brewer: I’m looking at my little sister’s high school class now, and i guess it just seems like all motivation to learn anything has gone completely out the window. All her teachers lesson plans are Chat generated. All the students essays are chat generated. Just seems to me like some systemic change to the system is necessary.

Those who are genuinely curious people will 10-100x their ability to learn. The opposite however is also true, the bottom 95% of learners will use Chat to skip work completely. Just sad to see a tool like this be used to escape critical thought by all parties involved. Curious how we fix this

Pizza: The internet gave every single person on Earth access to all of MIT’s lectures for free and I think most of us would agree that it hasn’t made us that much smarter. I don’t think the main problems and solutions here are technological.

All of YouTube, by contrast, did often make people either smarter or dumber, depending on how they used it, because it was far easier to use. MIT’s classes had too many trivial inconveniences and also tend to be actually quite hard.

If you want to learn a language in a month and are willing to put in the time and effort, you can probably do that right now, using a mixture of existing technology and LLMs. No one does it because no one both has that kind of time and wants to do that level of work.

claims.claim:
They Took Our Jobs

In response to the AI slop nonsense article from Chamath, Bryan Johnson tries to say the thing in actual human words.

Bryan Johnson: He's arguing that these knee jerk intuitions are wrong:

+ work is a fixed amount
+ machines doing tasks means lost jobs
+ cheaper things get used less
+ labor is the scarce resource
+ abundant intelligence removes human work
+ renting generic intelligence builds an edge

Elon Musk: AI+Robots will be able to do everything, resulting in universal high income. Work will be optional.

That’s good clear writing that isn’t full of Fnords, illustrating both the extent to which Chamath is using AI to argue with a strawman versus making meaningful claims, with the caveat that the strawman position on many of these questions is real and often popular.

claims.claim:
The true versions of the claims:

Work expands to fill the time allotted, with decreasing marginal returns.

Machines doing too many of the tasks means loss of the particular job in question.

Controlling for quality of the thing, cheaper things get used more, and total amount paid can go up or go down.

Labor is paid well if and only if it is the scarce resource, which it may not be.

Abundant intelligence increasingly removes human cognitive work, and can potentially lead to machines that increasingly remove human physical work.

Renting generic intelligence may or may not be part of a winning strategy, but paying to develop specialized intelligence likely gets you bitter lesson pilled.

I would focus on ‘labor is the scarce resource.’

claims.claim:
Is AI already net killing jobs?

The lived experience and anecdotes say yes, at least at entry level. The economics types keep trying to quote statistics to try and say no.

Ara Kharazian: We can finally say AI isn't killing jobs.

A new paper from me, @tryramp , and @RevelioLabs uses firm-level spend and workforce data across 21K U.S. businesses to measure AI's impact on jobs.

Firms that adopt AI heavily grow headcount 10% over two years following adoption. Low adopters see no statistically significant change.

passages.why: Foster compares F1 to AI-generated work

passages.text:
F1 was well-executed, zero-perplexity, hallucination-filled not-technically-AI slop. Brad Pitt does the Brad Pitt thing and oozes cool. The people liked it.

I say ‘not technically AI’ because it was made by an intelligence that was rather artificial in its own way, except it was instantiated inside humans.

I did not like F1, because it fell under my Obvious Slop waterline and the theoretical sport it was portraying, that is very different from F1, was neither coherent nor safe. Jodie Foster is correct, as is the parallel to AI.
passages.why: The author critiques F1 as artificial slop

passages.text:
One possibility is this leads to bifurcation.

If you are making a generic low-perplexity movie or other piece of media, you can let the AI cook, and you will get your delicious pile of slop.

If you are making a high-perplexity movie or other piece of media, that works with its restrictions and says and does actual things, then you will use AI at most with caution, and part of the experience will be knowing it is not AI.
passages.why: Predicts a split in media production

claims.claim: 20The full story of Rezső Kasztner is too complex to get into here, but at a high level: the “Kasztner trial” began as a libel case against a pamphleteer who had accused him of collaboration, but became a public reckoning over Kasztner himself; the trial court largely condemned him, the Israeli Supreme Court later partly exonerated him, and Kasztner was assassinated before the appeal was decided. The trial scandalized the young nation and ended up bringing down the Israeli government. One particularly damning detail: Kasztner served as a character witness for Eichmann even after the war, when he presumably had nothing to gain from it.

Using Sex for Ideological Compliance

There are documented cases of cults using sex for recruitment and ideological control. Weird sex, and weird power dynamics around sex are very common in cults. They are, of course, common in this one, too.

passages.text:
You remember Jacob Coxon? The “whistleblower” who resigned from Anthropic, and then “whistleblew” that all the things Anthropic already preaches are true? We had him at the beginning of this post, giving a long explanation about how much he respects rationalists to Ed Zitron.

Here’s Aella, three days before he went public, promising to throw whoever it is a “reverse gangbang” if they will quit from a lab and whistleblow. (People keeping asking me what a reverse gangbang is: one man, many women).

Here she is on the day of:

I am supposed to believe this is a coincidence, because I am supposed to believe that everything is a coincidence.

passages.text:
Recruiting Women Into Sex Work

This is public knowledge. At least 1800 people as of the time that screenshot was taken were aware of this fact. Essentially everyone in the scene knows this. It is a joke, a meme, played for laughs. claims.claim:
The part of the FTX empire that handled its weird charitable donations was called FTX Future Fund. Donations to CFAR would naturally have been within this organization’s responsibilities. These donations were made between March 3, 2022 and Oct 3, 2022. The entire team resigned on November 10th, professing to be shocked and immensely saddened to learn of recent events.

I believe they were saddened, but I don’t believe they were shocked. They are:

Nick Beckstead (Secure AI Project, CEO and co-founder. Coefficient Giving funded.)

Leopold Aschenbrenner (Situational Awareness hedge fund, rumored to be under investigation by the SEC)

Avital Balwit (Anthropic, Chief of Staff)

Ketan Ramakrishnan (I Have No Idea Who This Is)

Will MacAskill (He’s William Fucking MacAskill, one of the initial founders of Effective Altruism, a cofounder of Giving What We Can, the Centre for Effective Altruism and 80,000 Hours)

Aella is a prostitute, former camgirl, and person who is very good at the internet. She is also the on-again, off-again girlfriend of the President of MIRI, Nate Soares. She thrives on shock reactions, and seems unique so far in history for having used the social camouflage of being edgy on the internet to get away with as much as she has while operating almost completely in the open. Everything she does seems to be just up to the line, and there is always some defense that sort of makes sense at the time. It is incredible that she is this good at controlling and navigating the information environment. She is perhaps the first truly social media native predator of this kind or magnitude.

passages.text:
The Ghislaine Maxwell of Silicon Valley

Aella is a prostitute, former camgirl, and person who is very good at the internet. She is also the on-again, off-again girlfriend of the President of MIRI, Nate Soares. She thrives on shock reactions, and seems unique so far in history for having used the social camouflage of being edgy on the internet to get away with as much as she has while operating almost completely in the open. Everything she does seems to be just up to the line, and there is always some defense that sort of makes sense at the time. It is incredible that she is this good at controlling and navigating the information environment. She is perhaps the first truly social media native predator of this kind or magnitude.
passages.why: Characterizes Aella and her public persona

passages.text: As the scene has spiralled and become more bizarre, she has come to seem like a major cultural leader, if not the main cultural leader of rationalism. I see her posts more, she headlines their Woodstock (there’s a rationalist woodstock! it is called vibecamp), and of course she organizes many of their orgies, which appear to be the social glue holding a lot of this together.
passages.why: Describes Aella’s influence in rationalist culture

passages.text: One of the interesting things about cults is that the men are usually the leaders, figureheads, thinkers, and the public face of the organization, but often the actual getting-shit-done part of the cult and arguably the real leadership that matters is done entirely by women. Jim Jones made almost none of the preparations for the Jonestown suicide. His lieutenants, who were women, ordered and prepared all the kool-aid and all the cyanide.
passages.why: Compares cult leadership roles and cites Jonestown

passages.text: Aella has a uniquely well-suited background for this role. She is the daughter of an abusive Calvinist preacher, and she escaped from that into atheism, LSD, social media and sex work. She has in turn made herself the primary sexual partner of Nate Soares, the president of MIRI, and the primary center of this cult’s sexual recruiting and practices. It is an almost perfectly Berkeley way of both inverting and becoming who she was raised to be.
passages.why: Connects Aella’s background to her alleged role

passages.text: She is good at bringing a voice to the cause. She has donated enough money to Lighthaven to have her name on a plaque, and to have walk-in privileges whenever she likes. Yudkowsky likes her, promotes her, legitimizes her internet sex surveys as a social scientist, sometimes attends her orgies, and puts her into the acknowledgements of his books.
passages.why: Describes Aella’s support and connections

passages.text:
Here she is talking about the overlap between AI safety and polyamory in the Bay. It is worth reproducing her post in full: “Yeah if you count casual relationships as connections, the ai safety community in the bay is probably a single polycule”

Here’s her opinion of a thread I wrote on this same subject earlier.

It’s good to know that fewer than 50% of attendees for any one of her orgies work in AI-related stuff.

Also, I never used the words “sex trafficking”.
passages.why: Quotes Aella and responds to criticism

passages.text:
Using Sex for Ideological Compliance

There are documented cases of cults using sex for recruitment and ideological control. Weird sex, and weird power dynamics around sex are very common in cults. They are, of course, common in this one, too.
passages.why: Claims sex is used for recruitment and control

passages.text:
You remember Jacob Coxon? The “whistleblower” who resigned from Anthropic, and then “whistleblew” that all the things Anthropic already preaches are true? We had him at the beginning of this post, giving a long explanation about how much he respects rationalists to Ed Zitron.

Here’s Aella, three days before he went public, promising to throw whoever it is a “reverse gangbang” if they will quit from a lab and whistleblow. (People keeping asking me what a reverse gangbang is: one man, many women).

Here she is on the day of:

I am supposed to believe this is a coincidence, because I am supposed to believe that everything is a coincidence.
passages.why: Links Aella’s offer to a lab whistleblower

passages.text: This is what she calls her finest piece of work, a Sankey diagram documenting the process for scheduling a large gangbang on her birthday. I insinuated that Yudkowsky may be represented in the graph, once, and she seemed to be trying to correct me, so probably he isn’t in this one even though he attends her other orgies. She says her “partner” set up the event, and one can reasonably infer that this means Nate Soares.
passages.why: Discusses Aella’s diagram and alleged connections

passages.text: Here she is explaining that she is giving what she can to the cause by filtering invites to her gangbang based upon ideology. (e/acc is a rival ideology to EA. I have historically hated it but increasingly feel like I would like Literally Any Ideology Other Than Effective Altruism)
passages.why: Claims Aella screens invitations by ideology

passages.text:
This is the banner for an article by Nicholas Decker from April 16, 2025, about overthrowing the United Stated government by force and/or violence.

This is Aella’s reward for that article.

I think we can conclusively say that she uses sex to promote her ideology.
passages.why: Argues Aella uses sex to promote an ideology

passages.text:
Recruiting Women Into Sex Work

This is public knowledge. At least 1800 people as of the time that screenshot was taken were aware of this fact. Essentially everyone in the scene knows this. It is a joke, a meme, played for laughs. We are not sufficiently accepting of her profession and identity if we have a problem with it. It should not trouble us that she is a major public face of a religious movement that specifically appeals to the overwhelmingly young and vulnerable sort of person who moves to San Francisco over fan fiction.

She also recruited her sisters as cam girls once. I am vague on the details.

Her sisters will come up again later.
passages.why: Discusses Aella recruiting women into sex work

passages.text: It seems maybe credible that she has never taken a direct financial cut from anyone’s sex work whom she recruited. It is somewhat less credible that she has never indirectly benefitted. It seems, however, likely that she has been recruiting people into sex work overwhelmingly because she enjoys doing it and somewhat because it is what she can do for the cause. Ghislaine Maxwell wasn’t paid for her work. Money is not why these people do these things.
passages.why: Speculates about Aella’s motives and benefits

claims.claim: Lighthaven is formerly the Rose Garden Inn. It has four main buildings, abundant outdoor space, and it’s a beautiful place. I suspect its name was meant to echo Greyhaven, which is the name Marion Zimmer Bradley gave her home.
claims.context: Lighthaven is formerly the Rose Garden Inn. It has four main buildings, abundant outdoor space, and it’s a beautiful place. I suspect its name was meant to echo Greyhaven, which is the name Marion Zimmer Bradley gave her home.

claims.claim:
It was originally purchased with money wired to CFAR from Sam Bankman-Fried’s company, FTX, as it was collapsing. This was later found to be fraudulent: Bankman-Fried and his employees looted the company because they knew it was dying and sent as much cash as they could to their friends and to causes they believed in.

One of those causes was that the Bay Area Rationalist and Effective Altruist community should have its own permanent conference center.

claims.claim:
I am expected to believe that Sam Bankman-Fried was not a true believer. I am expected to believe that he was not central to Effective Altruism. I am expected to believe that committing ten billion dollars of fraud was not in accordance with the values of Effective Altruism.

This is all bullshit. He was giving what he could to the cause. Now he is being a good soldier and disowning the cause to protect it, and he is doing his twenty-five years. I respect it. It is the only respectable thing about him.

claims.claim:
The part of the FTX empire that handled its weird charitable donations was called FTX Future Fund. Donations to CFAR would naturally have been within this organization’s responsibilities. These donations were made between March 3, 2022 and Oct 3, 2022. The entire team resigned on November 10th, professing to be shocked and immensely saddened to learn of recent events.

I believe they were saddened, but I don’t believe they were shocked. They are:

Nick Beckstead (Secure AI Project, CEO and co-founder. Coefficient Giving funded.)

Leopold Aschenbrenner (Situational Awareness hedge fund, rumored to be under investigation by the SEC)

Avital Balwit (Anthropic, Chief of Staff)

Ketan Ramakrishnan (I Have No Idea Who This Is)

Will MacAskill (He’s William Fucking MacAskill, one of the initial founders of Effective Altruism, a cofounder of Giving What We Can, the Centre for Effective Altruism and 80,000 Hours)

claims.claim:
In 2022 they spun out a separate organization from CFAR called Lightcone Infrastructure, which has exactly two responsibilities: managing Lighthaven, and running LessWrong. As far as Rationalist and Effective Altruist are ever separate things in the Bay, Lighthaven is Rationalist.

Lighthaven’s initial funding, however, was Effective Altruist, and most of the events held there are Effective Altruist.

passages.text: Lighthaven is formerly the Rose Garden Inn. It has four main buildings, abundant outdoor space, and it’s a beautiful place. I suspect its name was meant to echo Greyhaven, which is the name Marion Zimmer Bradley gave her home.

passages.text:
It was originally purchased with money wired to CFAR from Sam Bankman-Fried’s company, FTX, as it was collapsing. This was later found to be fraudulent: Bankman-Fried and his employees looted the company because they knew it was dying and sent as much cash as they could to their friends and to causes they believed in.

One of those causes was that the Bay Area Rationalist and Effective Altruist community should have its own permanent conference center.

passages.text:
I am expected to believe that Sam Bankman-Fried was not a true believer. I am expected to believe that he was not central to Effective Altruism. I am expected to believe that committing ten billion dollars of fraud was not in accordance with the values of Effective Altruism.

This is all bullshit. He was giving what he could to the cause. Now he is being a good soldier and disowning the cause to protect it, and he is doing his twenty-five years. I respect it. It is the only respectable thing about him.
passages.why: Argues Bankman-Fried acted for Effective Altruism

passages.text: It is fucking unbelievable how good these people are at disowning their failures, and how reliably their failures fall on their swords to protect everyone else. They don’t have to be told: they simply know that it’s what they need to do.

passages.text:
The part of the FTX empire that handled its weird charitable donations was called FTX Future Fund. Donations to CFAR would naturally have been within this organization’s responsibilities. These donations were made between March 3, 2022 and Oct 3, 2022. The entire team resigned on November 10th, professing to be shocked and immensely saddened to learn of recent events.

I believe they were saddened, but I don’t believe they were shocked. They are:

Nick Beckstead (Secure AI Project, CEO and co-founder. Coefficient Giving funded.)

Leopold Aschenbrenner (Situational Awareness hedge fund, rumored to be under investigation by the SEC)

Avital Balwit (Anthropic, Chief of Staff)

Ketan Ramakrishnan (I Have No Idea Who This Is)

Will MacAskill (He’s William Fucking MacAskill, one of the initial founders of Effective Altruism, a cofounder of Giving What We Can, the Centre for Effective Altruism and 80,000 Hours)
passages.why: Names Future Fund staff and questions their surprise

passages.text:
The Ghislaine Maxwell of Silicon Valley

Aella is a prostitute, former camgirl, and person who is very good at the internet. She is also the on-again, off-again girlfriend of the President of MIRI, Nate Soares. She thrives on shock reactions, and seems unique so far in history for having used the social camouflage of being edgy on the internet to get away with as much as she has while operating almost completely in the open. Everything she does seems to be just up to the line, and there is always some defense that sort of makes sense at the time. It is incredible that she is this good at controlling and navigating the information environment. She is perhaps the first truly social media native predator of this kind or magnitude.
passages.why: Characterizes Aella and her public persona

passages.text: As the scene has spiralled and become more bizarre, she has come to seem like a major cultural leader, if not the main cultural leader of rationalism. I see her posts more, she headlines their Woodstock (there’s a rationalist woodstock! it is called vibecamp), and of course she organizes many of their orgies, which appear to be the social glue holding a lot of this together.
passages.why: Claims Aella leads rationalist social life

passages.text: One of the interesting things about cults is that the men are usually the leaders, figureheads, thinkers, and the public face of the organization, but often the actual getting-shit-done part of the cult and arguably the real leadership that matters is done entirely by women. Jim Jones made almost none of the preparations for the Jonestown suicide. His lieutenants, who were women, ordered and prepared all the kool-aid and all the cyanide.
passages.why: Compares cult leadership roles and Jonestown

passages.text: Aella has a uniquely well-suited background for this role. She is the daughter of an abusive Calvinist preacher, and she escaped from that into atheism, LSD, social media and sex work. She has in turn made herself the primary sexual partner of Nate Soares, the president of MIRI, and the primary center of this cult’s sexual recruiting and practices. It is an almost perfectly Berkeley way of both inverting and becoming who she was raised to be.
passages.why: Connects Aella’s background to alleged recruitment

passages.text: She is good at bringing a voice to the cause. She has donated enough money to Lighthaven to have her name on a plaque, and to have walk-in privileges whenever she likes. Yudkowsky likes her, promotes her, legitimizes her internet sex surveys as a social scientist, sometimes attends her orgies, and puts her into the acknowledgements of his books.
passages.why: Describes Aella’s ties to Lighthaven and Yudkowsky

claims.claim:
Paperclips, Doom

Yudkowsky’s most viral idea, the one that infects the most people and spreads the farthest, is that AI, if we continue to develop it, will

certainly recursively self-improve, quickly achieving superintelligence (”RSI”),

certainly escape human control,

certainly kill everyone (”paperclip them”, “doom”).

claims.claim: All arguments about AI Safety and AI Alignment are primarily about mitigating this exact scenario under his exact terms. Significant modification is relatively rare. Where lower probabilities of doom than “certain” are given, people seem to still generally worry exclusively about Yudkowsky’s rough scenario: a sudden, unpredictable sequence of 1) superintelligence, 2) immediate escape from control, and 3) the death of all humans on Earth. This is always, implicitly, what "safety" and "alignment" are about.

In 1996, a 17-year-old Eliezer Yudkowsky joins Usenet and the Extropians mailing list. His more notable influences are Drexler’s book on nanotechnology, Kurzweil’s book on AI, and Nick Bostrom, who frequents the Extropians mailing list. (Usenet was still largely full of academics). In 1998, Nick Bostrom argues that a superintelligent AI might not necessarily be good or friendly, which along with other of Bostrom’s ideas will later become core to Yudkowsky.

claims.claim: In the year 2000, Yudkowsky founds the Singularity Institute for Artificial Intelligence, SIAI, later renamed to the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, MIRI. This appears to have started as a fake-it-til-you-make-it sort of thing, and it doesn’t pick up until he gets sponsored by Peter Thiel. Peter Thiel will be his largest sponsor until about 2015 or 2016. Now in 2026, Thiel has long since cut all ties, called this scene a “burning man camp” and “Luddite”, and called Yudkowsky the Antichrist.4

passages.text: In spite of being often considered disgraceful and now being somewhat starved for cash, Yudkowsky and the organizations most closely tied to him are still, by far, the most influential sources of thinking about AI safety in the Bay and therefore on Earth. Because so many investors and key staff members hold him and his ideas in high regard, it is not clear that companies can directly disown him, although for example when Dario says to be less religious or less obsessed with “doom”, he appears to be positioning himself to try to carve influence away.
passages.why: Yudkowsky’s influence

passages.text:
Paperclips, Doom

Yudkowsky’s most viral idea, the one that infects the most people and spreads the farthest, is that AI, if we continue to develop it, will

certainly recursively self-improve, quickly achieving superintelligence (”RSI”),

certainly escape human control,

certainly kill everyone (”paperclip them”, “doom”).
passages.why: Describes Yudkowsky’s doom scenario

passages.text: All arguments about AI Safety and AI Alignment are primarily about mitigating this exact scenario under his exact terms. Significant modification is relatively rare. Where lower probabilities of doom than “certain” are given, people seem to still generally worry exclusively about Yudkowsky’s rough scenario: a sudden, unpredictable sequence of 1) superintelligence, 2) immediate escape from control, and 3) the death of all humans on Earth. This is always, implicitly, what "safety" and "alignment" are about.
passages.why: Claims this scenario dominates AI safety

passages.text: These ideas occasionally veer into believing AI is magic. When presented as serious science and policy, this sort of thing is omitted.
passages.why: Characterizes the ideas and their presentation

passages.text: Ordinarily, the play here would be to disown this and other concrete statements of his about AI doom as irrelevant. Of course we aren’t just repeating Yudkowsky! We are smart, normal people who believe normal things for normal reasons. Compare it, however, to AI 2027, allegedly a serious policy document, written by Daniel Kokotajlo and Scott Alexander, presenting its doom scenario.
passages.why: Compares AI 2027 to Yudkowsky’s ideas

passages.text: This is a genre of science fiction that has a doomsday cult built around it. There are only slight modifications to the basic belief system. Somehow, maybe by just throwing money at it, taking these ideas seriously has been rendered prestigious or at least not too disgraceful, such that Kokotajlo, credited on the above, gets to advise Bernie Sanders. JD Vance was asked about this piece by Ross Douthat at the New York Times, and said he had read it. (In my opinion, on close reading AI 2027’s primary intended audience was clearly JD Vance.)
passages.why: Critiques AI 2027’s genre and influence

passages.text: Essentially all of AI safety is rationalizations over Eliezer Yudkowsky’s ideas and there is no other substance to it. It is smokescreens, and Eliezer Yudkowsky.
passages.why: Claims AI safety derives from Yudkowsky

passages.text: This is his actual plan: to halt all AI research, all across the Earth, and instead do genetic engineering eugenics for a generation. Pause AI, stop AI, slowdown, pacing the frontier, they are all smokescreens, rationalizations, or ways of watering down this plan. This is why there is never any real “after we pause”, or “we will unpause when”; this is the only actual plan, and the public front for the plan cannot say this because it is too stupid and too offensive to be spoken in public, except by Yudkowsky, who never stops talking and who is too fucking ridiculous for anyone on the outside to believe everyone listens to him.
passages.why: Alleges Yudkowsky’s actual policy plan

passages.text: Anyone who thinks this is not the plan is not in on the plan, or is part of some faction that simply has no real plan. If this describes you and you didn’t know that, I am sorry that this is how you found out.
passages.why: Claims outsiders are unaware of the plan

passages.text: He has long since deleted this post demonstrating what his idea of an acceptable outcome is; this is ordinarily implied and not stated.
passages.why: Refers to a deleted post

passages.text: This industry approaches regulation in this way because it has, at its core, a millenarian death cult that worships and fears AI, believes AI will end the world, feels compelled to create AI, and at least somewhat wants to destroy AI as an entire field.
passages.why: Characterizes the industry’s approach to regulation

passages.text: I will repeat: I do not think that these people should be making policy. I would vastly prefer if this were merely some insane Bay Area drama that I could ignore, but this has been made a very public national and international concern.
passages.why: Opposes these people making policy

passages.text: The paperclip maximizer is a thought experiment from 2003 and of very little relevance at all. People are perpetually striving to find evidence for this theory because they already believe it is true, and take pains to interpret any research or security development in AI as evidence for this exact doom coming to pass. As things come up which contradict this scenario, as often they do, they are often not understood because they do not match the prophecy. Alternative explanations are so unthinkable that many people cannot even be told.
passages.why: Critiques paperclip-maximizer reasoning

passages.text: Doom seems to be the most infectious idea here because it activates the same neurosis that every apocalyptic or millenarian cult does. The world is going to end, and only I and my special group of people in the know can maybe stop it. (Also, you should give me money and have sex with me.)
passages.why: Explains doom’s appeal as cult-like

passages.text: You can argue with them in any way you like but it barely matters. It's not, mostly, something people believe for good reasons, and they will simply go back to complaining about the apocalypse as soon as you stop paying attention. There are enough of them that the belief is self-reinforcing; they can arrange their lives such that they essentially never talk to anyone who is not a believer.
passages.why: Claims the belief is self-reinforcing

passages.text: Harry Potter fan fiction, of course, is especially popular with children, and many people have made this their belief system since they were teenagers.
passages.why: Links the movement to teenage interests

passages.text: Since recruitment largely happens on the internet, people are widely dispersed. Where they are gathered in person, it is mostly in various communes in Berkeley, California. They call their communes "group houses", maybe to make it sound less cultish. Most of the details of this are what you expect from "a commune in Berkeley".
passages.why: Describes recruitment and communal living

passages.text: Everyone is polyamorous, everyone attends the same events, everyone lives in group homes together, everyone venerates the same few authors, everyone is very worried about AI doom, and a lot of people are on psychedelic drugs. They are all very contrarian together.
passages.why: Characterizes the community

passages.text: Lots and lots of them work at AI companies and non-profits. The safety, red team and alignment teams seem especially afflicted, because that's the area you go on to worry about and try to work against AI doom, which you are sure is at least medium likely. Other members will seek work in finance, because Effective Altruism, by creed, says you should seek more money so you can give more to charity. Those most concerned with AI risk will tend to almost exclusively give to AI charities and not any other Effective Altruist concern.
passages.why: Describes members’ work and charitable giving

passages.text: As a whole, this is a religious movement. Not everyone takes marching orders; they’re united by an idea, not any particular structure. The vast network of Effective Altruists around the world working on other charitable concerns are basically irrelevant to AI Safety. The core people who mostly live together and attend events and especially orgies in Berkeley are a sex cult, and the ones that aren't directly involved are part of the wider movement and are first and foremost its recruiting funnel, funding, and labor base.
passages.why: Describes the movement’s structure

passages.text: Any time you get more than a few people who are deeply concerned with AI doom together, it seems like their natural form of organization looks like a cult; the movement as a whole, internationally, is less of a cult than it is a cult factory. Some of these cults have gone very badly. One of them is the Zizians.
passages.why: Claims AI-doom groups form cults

passages.text: That rationalists form cults constantly has been previously examined. There are many causative factors, but the core one is just that the entire thing is, in and of childhood, a millenarian doomsday cult. If you believe you’re saving the world, it justifies anything; you cannot go against the cause for any reason. This gives leaders, whether official or unofficial, immense power over their members.
passages.why: Explains why the author says cults form

passages.text: Forming a separate cult is also how you carve off influence and ultimately power for yourself, separate from the wider movement. This tends to mean that people try to do it more. All of these power struggles make the details of all of this extremely noisy, chaotic, and difficult to explain.
passages.why: Connects cult formation to power struggles

passages.text: When you cut through all the distractions, chaos, and power struggles, San Francisco Rationalism is the inner circle of San Francisco Effective Altruism, which is the inner circle of Effective Altruism globally. Power and especially intellectual leadership flow almost entirely outwards from SF Rationalism to SF Effective Altruism to Effective Altruism’s global AI safety efforts. Everything else about Effective Altruism is effectively a front.
passages.why: Claims a hierarchy within Effective Altruism

passages.text: All of this has been an open secret for years. Everyone knows. Everyone knows if they say anything it will be ignored. I am shocked that I have gotten as much attention as I have to the problem; so let me try to get everything that seems to be very important into the record.
passages.why: Introduces the author’s account

passages.text:
A Brief History of Rationalism

What I am hoping to convey is that this is not many small things, it’s one big thing. All of this is tied together through ideology, funding, and key people.

Bay Area rationalists and effective altruists do not document their own history because it is disgraceful. Only their enemies deliberately keep records of what they have done and are doing.

They do however write constantly, but they do this mostly as a social activity. They have been writing essays, chattering, bragging, or engaging in some kind of drama constantly for the last fifteen years.

So you really just have to read a lot to put this together.3 Everything I am saying, as far as I am capable, is true, and I believe the vast majority is public record. I am just connecting the dots by putting one straight line through them.
passages.why: Frames the history as one connected account

passages.why: Section heading

passages.text:
Yudkowsky’s most viral idea, the one that infects the most people and spreads the farthest, is that AI, if we continue to develop it, will

certainly recursively self-improve, quickly achieving superintelligence (”RSI”),

certainly escape human control,

certainly kill everyone (”paperclip them”, “doom”).
passages.why: Describes Yudkowsky’s AI-doom scenario

passages.text: All arguments about AI Safety and AI Alignment are primarily about mitigating this exact scenario under his exact terms. Significant modification is relatively rare. Where lower probabilities of doom than “certain” are given, people seem to still generally worry exclusively about Yudkowsky’s rough scenario: a sudden, unpredictable sequence of 1) superintelligence, 2) immediate escape from control, and 3) the death of all humans on Earth. This is always, implicitly, what "safety" and "alignment" are about.
passages.why: Characterizes AI safety discourse

passages.text: These ideas occasionally veer into believing AI is magic. When presented as serious science and policy, this sort of thing is omitted.
passages.why: Claims about AI-safety beliefs

passages.text: Ordinarily, the play here would be to disown this and other concrete statements of his about AI doom as irrelevant. Of course we aren’t just repeating Yudkowsky! We are smart, normal people who believe normal things for normal reasons. Compare it, however, to AI 2027, allegedly a serious policy document, written by Daniel Kokotajlo and Scott Alexander, presenting its doom scenario.
passages.why: Compares AI 2027 with Yudkowsky’s ideas

passages.text: This is a genre of science fiction that has a doomsday cult built around it. There are only slight modifications to the basic belief system. Somehow, maybe by just throwing money at it, taking these ideas seriously has been rendered prestigious or at least not too disgraceful, such that Kokotajlo, credited on the above, gets to advise Bernie Sanders. JD Vance was asked about this piece by Ross Douthat at the New York Times, and said he had read it. (In my opinion, on close reading AI 2027’s primary intended audience was clearly JD Vance.)
passages.why: Claims about AI 2027 and its influence

passages.text: Essentially all of AI safety is rationalizations over Eliezer Yudkowsky’s ideas and there is no other substance to it. It is smokescreens, and Eliezer Yudkowsky.
passages.why: Characterizes AI safety as a field

passages.text: This is his actual plan: to halt all AI research, all across the Earth, and instead do genetic engineering eugenics for a generation. Pause AI, stop AI, slowdown, pacing the frontier, they are all smokescreens, rationalizations, or ways of watering down this plan. This is why there is never any real “after we pause”, or “we will unpause when”; this is the only actual plan, and the public front for the plan cannot say this because it is too stupid and too offensive to be spoken in public, except by Yudkowsky, who never stops talking and who is too fucking ridiculous for anyone on the outside to believe everyone listens to him.
passages.why: Alleges Yudkowsky’s underlying plan

passages.text: Anyone who thinks this is not the plan is not in on the plan, or is part of some faction that simply has no real plan. If this describes you and you didn’t know that, I am sorry that this is how you found out.
passages.why: Claims about factions and the alleged plan

passages.text: He has long since deleted this post demonstrating what his idea of an acceptable outcome is; this is ordinarily implied and not stated.
passages.why: Refers to a deleted post

passages.text: This industry approaches regulation in this way because it has, at its core, a millenarian death cult that worships and fears AI, believes AI will end the world, feels compelled to create AI, and at least somewhat wants to destroy AI as an entire field.
passages.why: Explains the industry’s regulatory approach

passages.text: I will repeat: I do not think that these people should be making policy. I would vastly prefer if this were merely some insane Bay Area drama that I could ignore, but this has been made a very public national and international concern.
passages.why: Policy opinion and public significance

passages.text: The paperclip maximizer is a thought experiment from 2003 and of very little relevance at all. People are perpetually striving to find evidence for this theory because they already believe it is true, and take pains to interpret any research or security development in AI as evidence for this exact doom coming to pass. As things come up which contradict this scenario, as often they do, they are often not understood because they do not match the prophecy. Alternative explanations are so unthinkable that many people cannot even be told.
passages.why: Critiques the paperclip-maximizer idea

passages.text: Doom seems to be the most infectious idea here because it activates the same neurosis that every apocalyptic or millenarian cult does. The world is going to end, and only I and my special group of people in the know can maybe stop it. (Also, you should give me money and have sex with me.)
passages.why: Explains the appeal of doomsday beliefs

passages.text: You can argue with them in any way you like but it barely matters. It's not, mostly, something people believe for good reasons, and they will simply go back to complaining about the apocalypse as soon as you stop paying attention. There are enough of them that the belief is self-reinforcing; they can arrange their lives such that they essentially never talk to anyone who is not a believer.
passages.why: Describes believers and their social reinforcement

passages.text: Harry Potter fan fiction, of course, is especially popular with children, and many people have made this their belief system since they were teenagers.
passages.why: Claims about members’ early involvement

passages.text: Since recruitment largely happens on the internet, people are widely dispersed. Where they are gathered in person, it is mostly in various communes in Berkeley, California. They call their communes "group houses", maybe to make it sound less cultish. Most of the details of this are what you expect from "a commune in Berkeley".
passages.why: Describes recruitment and in-person communities

passages.text: Everyone is polyamorous, everyone attends the same events, everyone lives in group homes together, everyone venerates the same few authors, everyone is very worried about AI doom, and a lot of people are on psychedelic drugs. They are all very contrarian together.
passages.why: Characterizes the community’s lifestyle

passages.text: Lots and lots of them work at AI companies and non-profits. The safety, red team and alignment teams seem especially afflicted, because that's the area you go on to worry about and try to work against AI doom, which you are sure is at least medium likely. Other members will seek work in finance, because Effective Altruism, by creed, says you should seek more money so you can give more to charity. Those most concerned with AI risk will tend to almost exclusively give to AI charities and not any other Effective Altruist concern.
passages.why: Describes careers and charitable giving

passages.text: As a whole, this is a religious movement. Not everyone takes marching orders; they’re united by an idea, not any particular structure. The vast network of Effective Altruists around the world working on other charitable concerns are basically irrelevant to AI Safety. The core people who mostly live together and attend events and especially orgies in Berkeley are a sex cult, and the ones that aren't directly involved are part of the wider movement and are first and foremost its recruiting funnel, funding, and labor base.
passages.why: Characterizes the movement and its organization

passages.text: Any time you get more than a few people who are deeply concerned with AI doom together, it seems like their natural form of organization looks like a cult; the movement as a whole, internationally, is less of a cult than it is a cult factory. Some of these cults have gone very badly. One of them is the Zizians.
passages.why: Claims that AI-doom groups form cults

passages.text: That rationalists form cults constantly has been previously examined. There are many causative factors, but the core one is just that the entire thing is, in and of childhood, a millenarian doomsday cult. If you believe you’re saving the world, it justifies anything; you cannot go against the cause for any reason. This gives leaders, whether official or unofficial, immense power over their members.
passages.why: Explains the causes and power dynamics of cults

passages.text: Forming a separate cult is also how you carve off influence and ultimately power for yourself, separate from the wider movement. This tends to mean that people try to do it more. All of these power struggles make the details of all of this extremely noisy, chaotic, and difficult to explain.
passages.why: Describes cult formation and power struggles

passages.text: When you cut through all the distractions, chaos, and power struggles, San Francisco Rationalism is the inner circle of San Francisco Effective Altruism, which is the inner circle of Effective Altruism globally. Power and especially intellectual leadership flow almost entirely outwards from SF Rationalism to SF Effective Altruism to Effective Altruism’s global AI safety efforts. Everything else about Effective Altruism is effectively a front.
passages.why: Describes the alleged hierarchy of influence

passages.text:
Paperclips, Doom

Yudkowsky’s most viral idea, the one that infects the most people and spreads the farthest, is that AI, if we continue to develop it, will

certainly recursively self-improve, quickly achieving superintelligence (”RSI”),

certainly escape human control,

certainly kill everyone (”paperclip them”, “doom”).
passages.why: Describes Yudkowsky’s AI-doom scenario

passages.text:
All arguments about AI Safety and AI Alignment are primarily about mitigating this exact scenario under his exact terms. Significant modification is relatively rare. Where lower probabilities of doom than “certain” are given, people seem to still generally worry exclusively about Yudkowsky’s rough scenario: a sudden, unpredictable sequence of 1) superintelligence, 2) immediate escape from control, and 3) the death of all humans on Earth. This is always, implicitly, what "safety" and "alignment" are about.

These ideas occasionally veer into believing AI is magic. When presented as serious science and policy, this sort of thing is omitted.
passages.why: Claims AI-safety discourse centers on this scenario

passages.text: Ordinarily, the play here would be to disown this and other concrete statements of his about AI doom as irrelevant. Of course we aren’t just repeating Yudkowsky! We are smart, normal people who believe normal things for normal reasons. Compare it, however, to AI 2027, allegedly a serious policy document, written by Daniel Kokotajlo and Scott Alexander, presenting its doom scenario.
passages.why: Compares AI 2027 with Yudkowsky’s scenario

passages.text: This is a genre of science fiction that has a doomsday cult built around it. There are only slight modifications to the basic belief system. Somehow, maybe by just throwing money at it, taking these ideas seriously has been rendered prestigious or at least not too disgraceful, such that Kokotajlo, credited on the above, gets to advise Bernie Sanders. JD Vance was asked about this piece by Ross Douthat at the New York Times, and said he had read it. (In my opinion, on close reading AI 2027’s primary intended audience was clearly JD Vance.)
passages.why: Characterizes AI 2027 and its reception

passages.text: Essentially all of AI safety is rationalizations over Eliezer Yudkowsky’s ideas and there is no other substance to it. It is smokescreens, and Eliezer Yudkowsky.
passages.why: Claims AI safety is built on Yudkowsky’s ideas

passages.text: This is his actual plan: to halt all AI research, all across the Earth, and instead do genetic engineering eugenics for a generation. Pause AI, stop AI, slowdown, pacing the frontier, they are all smokescreens, rationalizations, or ways of watering down this plan. This is why there is never any real “after we pause”, or “we will unpause when”; this is the only actual plan, and the public front for the plan cannot say this because it is too stupid and too offensive to be spoken in public, except by Yudkowsky, who never stops talking and who is too fucking ridiculous for anyone on the outside to believe everyone listens to him.
passages.why: Alleges Yudkowsky’s underlying plan

passages.text: Anyone who thinks this is not the plan is not in on the plan, or is part of some faction that simply has no real plan. If this describes you and you didn’t know that, I am sorry that this is how you found out.
passages.why: Claims dissenters are uninformed or factional

passages.text: I will repeat: I do not think that these people should be making policy. I would vastly prefer if this were merely some insane Bay Area drama that I could ignore, but this has been made a very public national and international concern.
passages.why: Argues against these people making policy

passages.text: The paperclip maximizer is a thought experiment from 2003 and of very little relevance at all. People are perpetually striving to find evidence for this theory because they already believe it is true, and take pains to interpret any research or security development in AI as evidence for this exact doom coming to pass. As things come up which contradict this scenario, as often they do, they are often not understood because they do not match the prophecy. Alternative explanations are so unthinkable that many people cannot even be told.
passages.why: Criticizes interpretations of AI research

passages.text: Doom seems to be the most infectious idea here because it activates the same neurosis that every apocalyptic or millenarian cult does. The world is going to end, and only I and my special group of people in the know can maybe stop it. (Also, you should give me money and have sex with me.)
passages.why: Explains the appeal of AI-doom beliefs

passages.text: You can argue with them in any way you like but it barely matters. claims.claim:
In fact, most people in the community think doom is less likely than not. I’ve previously said that I think there’s about a 25-30% chance that AI drives humanity extinct. Geoffrey Hinton has said 10-50% chance. Dario Amodei has said 10-25%, Elon Musk 10-30%, and the average AI researcher in Grace’s 1,600 person sample said 18%.

There are some people who are more pessimistic; my AI 2027 co-author Daniel Kokotajlo says 70-80%, and Eliezer Yudkowsky says 90%+. But both of these people have devoted their lives to fighting back, which is the opposite of calling it inevitable.

claims.claim:
2: You falsely portray the AI risk community as expecting a perfect omniscient omnipotent superintelligence that controls every atom in the universe.

Across the years, you have written things like

“[These arguments] depend on the premises that humans are so gifted that they can design an omniscient and omnipotent AI” (source)

“They assumed that human engineers would grant [AIs] unlimited and irreversible control over the earth’s physical infrastructure, amounting to omnipotence over every atom on the planet.” (source)

“Important not to confuse the notion of “general intelligence” from psychometrics … with the (somewhat mystical) notion bandied about in AI of omniscience and omnipotence.” (source)

“It will never be omniscient . . . it’ll never be omnipotent. That’s out of comic books or religion.” (source)

“There’s no system that could learn the position and velocity of every particle in the universe. So long as that is true, there can’t be an AI system that can do anything or know everything.” (source)

“When we put aside fantasies like foom, digital megalomania, instant omniscience, and perfect control of every molecule in the universe…” (source)

“From animals to dull humans to smart humans to AI to Artificial Superintelligence, the latter consisting of perfect omniscience.” (source)

…and many more statements along the same lines.

But not only is this not our belief, but we try hard to explicitly specify that we believe the opposite. From a wiki page on superintelligence by Eliezer Yudkowsky:

Superintelligences are still bounded … They are (presumably) not infinitely smart, infinitely fast, all-knowing, or able to achieve every describable outcome using their available resources and options … A superintelligence doesn’t know everything and can’t perfectly estimate every quantity … A superintelligence is not omnipotent and can’t obtain every describable outcome.

Every definition of superintelligence, from Bostrom’s to Yudkowsky’s to Good’s, agrees that a superintelligence is merely a mind which is significantly smarter than any human’s.

Nor are we motte-and-baileying here, pretending we don’t think it’s omnipotent, but then treating it as omnipotent anyway. In the AI 2027 scenario, we state that superintelligence is achieved in late 2027 or early 2028, but that it’s unable to cleanly eliminate humans at that time, because it can’t maintain the data centers on its own. It takes two years of plotting before the superintelligence is able to finally eliminate humanity while preserving its own existence.

Where I think you are getting this is that we’re uncomfortable saying that superintelligence definitely can’t do any specific non-physically-impossible thing. For example, in the 2010s, we argued that people needed to be prepared for superintelligence designing dangerous biological weapons. Many people objected that this was absurd, because bioweapon design was bottlenecked on the protein folding problem, and there was no way that even superintelligence could solve protein folding. Then in 2020 one of Demis Hassabis’ narrow pre-LLM AIs solved protein folding easily. See also this this essay.

But being uncomfortable asserting that superintelligence can’t do any specific thing is not the same as affirmatively asserting that superintelligence will be omniscient and omnipotent. The latter would of course be shituf, which is a sin.

4: You falsely represent studies and experts who disagree with you as being on your side.

For example, in your open letter to me, you wrote:

A 2025 Rand Corporation modelling analysis steel-manned the AI-extinction hypothesis by granting the assumption that AI had the objective to wipe out humanity, and concluded that there is “no describable scenario in which AI is conclusively an extinction threat to humanity”.

But the RAND study actually concluded the opposite of this. Rand proposed the statement that you quoted as its null hypothesis, ie the claim to be investigated.

After doing their investigation, they concluded that contrary to their null hypothesis, they “could not rule out the possibility” that AI was such an extinction threat.

…and recommended that policy-makers “continue to perform AI risk research, but maintain a wide focus on other risks in addition to extinction risk.”

Or consider your book, Enlightenment Now. You argued that we didn’t need to worry too hard about alignment, because it will happen naturally in the context of developing AI. You quoted AI expert Stuart Russell:

[AI] is developed incrementally, designed to satisfy multiple conditions, tested before it is implemented, and constantly tweaked for efficacy and safety. As the AI expert Stuart Russell puts it, “No one in civil engineering talks about ‘building bridges that don’t fall down.’ They just call it ‘building bridges.’” Likewise, he notes, AI that is beneficial rather than dangerous is simply AI.

Stuart Russell has devoted his life to studying AI alignment, and is now a full-time activist raising awareness of the apocalyptic dangers of superintelligence. His most recent contribution is an article in Newsweek warning about The Race To Human Extinction. When Russell says that there is no distinction between bridge capabilities and bridge safety, he’s not claiming that no extra research is needed to study alignment - otherwise he wouldn’t have founded the Center For Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence, probably the biggest academic alignment research center in the world. And he’s not saying that alignment research will happen naturally at whatever speed it has to: otherwise he wouldn’t have signed a petition calling for “a prohibition on the development of superintelligence”. Russell is saying that AI alignment is so important that it should be viewed as foundational to all AI research, the same way that to a first approximation the whole point of building bridges is figuring out whether they will fall down or not.

5: You employ weird pseudo-arguments that could prove anything

(source)

You argue that superintelligence is “meaningless” because “there’s no point at which it’s meaningful to say” that “yesterday we didn’t have superintelligence. Today we do have superintelligence.”

But this could disprove any concept. For example:

Age is meaningless. After all, there’s no point at which someone was young yesterday, but old today.

Height is meaningless. After all, there is no specific line where one centimeter below the line is short, but one centimeter above the line is tall.

Lakes don’t exist. After all, a puddle is not a lake. But there is no point at which adding one extra drop of water to a non-lake turns it into a lake.

Several people with philosophical backgrounds commented that this was the sorites argument, a well-known pseudo-paradox which shouldn’t be employed for real work.

6: You unfairly accuse us of “distracting from” AI’s mundane harms and near-term risks.

Again in the tweet that made me challenge you, you said that AI extinction scenarios “distract from the more mundane and realistic safety challenges”.

You expand on this theme in your book:

Humanity has a finite budget of resources, brainpower, and anxiety. You can’t worry about everything. Some of the threats facing us, like climate change and nuclear war, are unmistakable, and will require immense effort and ingenuity to mitigate. Folding them into a list of exotic scenarios with minuscule or unknown probabilities can only dilute the sense of urgency.

Even in your open letter, you say that our “obsession” with alignment distracts us from the problems AI is causing today, like hacking. So: are concerns about speculative distant risks offensive to the people whose lives are being harmed by AI right now?

That’s not what those people told me when I marched beside them at our joint protests. Or when I helped them coordinate political action campaigns. Or when I donated money to our joint candidates.

2: You falsely portray the AI risk community as expecting a perfect omniscient omnipotent superintelligence that controls every atom in the universe.

Across the years, you have written things like

“[These arguments] depend on the premises that humans are so gifted that they can design an omniscient and omnipotent AI” (source)

“They assumed that human engineers would grant [AIs] unlimited and irreversible control over the earth’s physical infrastructure, amounting to omnipotence over every atom on the planet.” (source)

“Important not to confuse the notion of “general intelligence” from psychometrics … with the (somewhat mystical) notion bandied about in AI of omniscience and omnipotence.” (source)

“It will never be omniscient . . . it’ll never be omnipotent. That’s out of comic books or religion.” (source)

“There’s no system that could learn the position and velocity of every particle in the universe. So long as that is true, there can’t be an AI system that can do anything or know everything.” (source)

“When we put aside fantasies like foom, digital megalomania, instant omniscience, and perfect control of every molecule in the universe…” (source)

“From animals to dull humans to smart humans to AI to Artificial Superintelligence, the latter consisting of perfect omniscience.” (source)

…and many more statements along the same lines.

But not only is this not our belief, but we try hard to explicitly specify that we believe the opposite. From a wiki page on superintelligence by Eliezer Yudkowsky:

Superintelligences are still bounded … They are (presumably) not infinitely smart, infinitely fast, all-knowing, or able to achieve every describable outcome using their available resources and options … A superintelligence doesn’t know everything and can’t perfectly estimate every quantity … A superintelligence is not omnipotent and can’t obtain every describable outcome.

Every definition of superintelligence, from Bostrom’s to Yudkowsky’s to Good’s, agrees that a superintelligence is merely a mind which is significantly smarter than any human’s.

Nor are we motte-and-baileying here, pretending we don’t think it’s omnipotent, but then treating it as omnipotent anyway. In the AI 2027 scenario, we state that superintelligence is achieved in late 2027 or early 2028, but that it’s unable to cleanly eliminate humans at that time, because it can’t maintain the data centers on its own. It takes two years of plotting before the superintelligence is able to finally eliminate humanity while preserving its own existence.

Where I think you are getting this is that we’re uncomfortable saying that superintelligence definitely can’t do any specific non-physically-impossible thing. For example, in the 2010s, we argued that people needed to be prepared for superintelligence designing dangerous biological weapons. Many people objected that this was absurd, because bioweapon design was bottlenecked on the protein folding problem, and there was no way that even superintelligence could solve protein folding. Then in 2020 one of Demis Hassabis’ narrow pre-LLM AIs solved protein folding easily. See also this this essay.

But being uncomfortable asserting that superintelligence can’t do any specific thing is not the same as affirmatively asserting that superintelligence will be omniscient and omnipotent. The latter would of course be shituf, which is a sin.
passages.why: Rejects the claim that AI-risk arguments assume omnipotence and explains bounded-superintelligence concerns.

For example, in the 2010s, we argued that people needed to be prepared for superintelligence designing dangerous biological weapons. Many people objected that this was absurd, because bioweapon design was bottlenecked on the protein folding problem, and there was no way that even superintelligence could solve protein folding. Then in 2020 one of Demis Hassabis’ narrow pre-LLM AIs solved protein folding easily. See also this this essay.

But being uncomfortable asserting that superintelligence can’t do any specific thing is not the same as affirmatively asserting that superintelligence will be omniscient and omnipotent. The latter would of course be shituf, which is a sin.

Yet these were the only three “experts” that Lehmann interviewed for her article. Based on this, she goes on to call the idea of superintelligence a “fantasy”, “kooky”, like a “magical wizard”.

Meanwhile, Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize and Turing Award winning inventor of modern AI, quit his job to become a full-time activist warning about the possibility of superintelligence destroying the world. Yoshua Bengio, another Turing Award winning inventor of modern AI, also did that. Ilya Sutskever, the former Chief Scientist of OpenAI who helped invent ChatGPT and the modern LLM, wrote that superintelligence “could lead to the disempowerment of humanity or even human extinction”, and quit his job at OpenAI to found a company called Safe Superintelligence. Paul Christiano, who invented RLHF and headed safety at the US government’s AISI, says he thinks there’s a 20-50% chance AI kills everyone, and quit his job to start the Alignment Research Center. Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, and Demis Hassabis - the latter two of whom are great AI researchers in their own right even aside from their business credentials - have all said or suggested that they think human extinction is a plausible outcome of their work. Katja Grace surveyed AI researchers who published at various important conferences and journals, and found that on average, her sample of 1,600 gave the proposition an 18% chance.

4: You falsely represent studies and experts who disagree with you as being on your side.

For example, in your open letter to me, you wrote:

A 2025 Rand Corporation modelling analysis steel-manned the AI-extinction hypothesis by granting the assumption that AI had the objective to wipe out humanity, and concluded that there is “no describable scenario in which AI is conclusively an extinction threat to humanity”.

But the RAND study actually concluded the opposite of this. Rand proposed the statement that you quoted as its null hypothesis, ie the claim to be investigated.

After doing their investigation, they concluded that contrary to their null hypothesis, they “could not rule out the possibility” that AI was such an extinction threat.

…and recommended that policy-makers “continue to perform AI risk research, but maintain a wide focus on other risks in addition to extinction risk.”

Or consider your book, Enlightenment Now. You argued that we didn’t need to worry too hard about alignment, because it will happen naturally in the context of developing AI. You quoted AI expert Stuart Russell:

[AI] is developed incrementally, designed to satisfy multiple conditions, tested before it is implemented, and constantly tweaked for efficacy and safety. As the AI expert Stuart Russell puts it, “No one in civil engineering talks about ‘building bridges that don’t fall down.’ They just call it ‘building bridges.’” Likewise, he notes, AI that is beneficial rather than dangerous is simply AI.

Stuart Russell has devoted his life to studying AI alignment, and is now a full-time activist raising awareness of the apocalyptic dangers of superintelligence. His most recent contribution is an article in Newsweek warning about The Race To Human Extinction. When Russell says that there is no distinction between bridge capabilities and bridge safety, he’s not claiming that no extra research is needed to study alignment - otherwise he wouldn’t have founded the Center For Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence, probably the biggest academic alignment research center in the world. And he’s not saying that alignment research will happen naturally at whatever speed it has to: otherwise he wouldn’t have signed a petition calling for “a prohibition on the development of superintelligence”. Russell is saying that AI alignment is so important that it should be viewed as foundational to all AI research, the same way that to a first approximation the whole point of building bridges is figuring out whether they will fall down or not.

5: You employ weird pseudo-arguments that could prove anything

(source)

You argue that superintelligence is “meaningless” because “there’s no point at which it’s meaningful to say” that “yesterday we didn’t have superintelligence. Today we do have superintelligence.”

But this could disprove any concept. For example:

Age is meaningless. After all, there’s no point at which someone was young yesterday, but old today.

Height is meaningless. After all, there is no specific line where one centimeter below the line is short, but one centimeter above the line is tall.

Lakes don’t exist. After all, a puddle is not a lake. But there is no point at which adding one extra drop of water to a non-lake turns it into a lake.

Several people with philosophical backgrounds commented that this was the sorites argument, a well-known pseudo-paradox which shouldn’t be employed for real work.
